items.content_text:
A busy Ooltewah intersection could soon see long-awaited improvements. 🚧
 Mayor Wamp announced a proposal to accept a $1.9 million bid for upgrades at Snow Hill Road and Short Tail Springs Road, addressing congestion and safety concerns identified through traffic studies and roadway safety audits. 
 One of the first major projects funded through the County Roads Improvement Fund, the bid came in more than $600,000 under budget. 
 Pending County Commission approval, construction is expected to begin in September.

items.title: Domestic violence doesn’t always leave bruises—but it can still be deadly. 😔 In No Visible Bruises, Rachel Louise Snyde...
items.content_text:
Domestic violence doesn’t always leave bruises—but it can still be deadly. 😔
 In No Visible Bruises, Rachel Louise Snyder pulls back the curtain on how abuse is often misunderstood, minimized, or missed entirely—by friends, communities, and even the systems meant to protect people. Through survivor stories and reporting with advocates and law enforcement, she shows how warning signs can hide in plain sight and why leaving isn’t a simple “just walk away” moment.
 The book also points to real, practical ways prevention and intervention can work—when we stop relying on myths and start taking patterns, risk, and safety seriously. 💜
 What’s one myth about domestic violence you’ve heard that you wish people would unlearn—and why? 🗣️
  🔗 https://zpr.io/Lh74aZA482mQ
 #NoVisibleBruises #EndDomesticViolence #DomesticViolenceAwareness #SurvivorVoices #DVBookClub

 Ever wondered what happens behind the scenes at the East Ridge Police Department? Now’s your chance to find out!
 The East Ridge Police Department Citizens’ Police Academy is now accepting applications for Class #26-01, beginning Tuesday, September 8, 2026.
 Over the course of the 10-week academy, participants will get an inside look at the many aspects of law enforcement and learn directly from members of ERPD. 
 Topics will include:
 🔹 Uniform Patrol
 🔹 Criminal Investigations
 🔹 Traffic Enforcement
 🔹 K-9 Unit
 🔹 Special Operations
 🔹 And much more!
 Beginning: September 8, 2026
 Every Tuesday: 6:00 PM – 9:00 PM
 Class Size: Limited to 12 participants
 Applications will be processed on a first-come, first-served basis, so don’t wait to sign up!
 📝 Application:
 https://www.eastridgetn.gov/uploads/police_5_356005280.pdf
 📝 Required Waiver:
 https://www.eastridgetn.gov/uploads/police_5_3411537685.pdf
 Completed forms may be returned to the East Ridge Police Department, 4214 Ringgold Road, Monday through Friday from 8:00am to 4:00pm. 
 The Citizens’ Police Academy is a great opportunity to learn more about what our officers do, why they do it, and how ERPD and the community can continue working together to make East Ridge an even better place to live.
 Ready to step behind the badge? We encourage you to apply today! 🚔

To: Mayor Lloyd and Collegedale City Commissioners
 From: Jon Holmes, City Manager
 Date: Friday, August 14, 2026
 RE: Weekly Update 08/10 – 08/14
 Administration – Jon Holmes, City Manager
 • Ongoing discussions with Chattanooga Gas regarding a Pressure Regulator Station infrastructure upgrade request and research 
 • Attended the Planning Commission Meeting
 • Work on grant application for the Tourism Enhancement Grant for TN Dept. of Tourism
 • Finalized School Resource Officer Agreement for Collegedale Academy
 • Research on Special Event policies and Procedures and application process
 • eCode360 went live on the City’s website; this is an online version of the City’s Municipal Code and is the most up-to-date version of the City of Collegedale’s City Code and it is regularly updated every 60 to 90 days with any changes or additions to the City Code. This is a huge step forward since our previous web host only did periodic updating. Citizens can register to get notifications whenever the City Code is updated and have access to the City Codes 24/7. The link is: https://ecode360.com/CO7135/laws

 • Website Redesign: Discussed design direction for Stage Two
 • Communications Survey: Sent out to gather feedback from the public on current communication
 Collegedale Airport – Ryan Byford
 • We replaced the keypad on our walk thru gate after the previous unit failed. 
 • Public Works has spent a great amount of time this week assisting with trimming and removing vegetation in the ditches around the property. They also re-striped our parking lot and the results look fantastic!
 • We have spent a significant amount of time this week on administrative tasks and follow up items from Friday’s ACIP meeting with TDOT. Our attendance will be needed at the Tennessee Aeronautics Commission in the coming months, once an engineer’s estimate can be determined on the PAPI project. The resultant cost is anticipated to require above $100,000 in State Funding.
 • TDOT spent some time explaining that funding for General Aviation in the State is becoming increasingly more limited, as it is now funded through direct appropriations from the State General Fund.

 Building Permits

 continuing to violate the sign ordinance.

School absences are a growing problem around the world, with rates in some countries nearly doubling since before COVID. 
 Attendance problems can be caused by issues inside and outside school, such as illness, mental health, family circumstances, poverty and safety. 
 Often the students who are long-term absent feel a lower sense of belonging at school, are bullied more and have worse academic outcomes.
 School attendance won't be fixed by enforcement alone. Schools also need to focus on creating environments where students feel safe, supported, and engaged in learning.

items.title: AI is moving fast. But behind all of that technology are some very basic resources: water, electricity, land and public...
items.content_text:
AI is moving fast. But behind all of that technology are some very basic resources: water, electricity, land and public infrastructure.
 And those resources are already under pressure.
 August is National Water Quality Month, which makes this a good time to talk about something that often gets lost in conversations about the AI boom: what happens to the communities where this infrastructure is being built?
 Across the South, Black communities are already dealing with aging water systems, pollution, higher energy burdens and decades of underinvestment.
 Now, Georgia and Texas are seeing data centers drive up demand for massive amounts of electricity and water. These projects can bring billions of dollars in private investment, but communities are left with important questions:
 How much water will these facilities use?
 How much electricity will they require?
 Who will pay for the infrastructure needed to support them?
 Who is getting the tax breaks?
 And what are the people who already live there getting in return?
 We’ve seen this story before.
 Black communities have too often been asked to carry the environmental and infrastructure costs of “economic development” while corporations and investors walk away with the biggest benefits.
 That’s why communities need a real seat at the table as the AI economy expands.
 The future is being built in our communities. The people who live there should have a say in what gets built, what it costs, and who benefits.
 #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #DataCenters #EnvironmentalJustice #BlackCommunities #ClimateJustice #WaterQuality #Infrastructure

 Reckless Endangerment (x2)
 Speeding
 Possession of Fentanyl
 Possession of Drug Paraphernalia
 Resisting Arrest

Parenting is one of the most important jobs, and no one should have to do it alone.
 Parents as Teachers (PAT) is a free, voluntary, evidence-based home visiting program designed to support families with young children. Recognizing that every family is unique, support is delivered directly to your home, where learning and development occur every day.
 Through regular home visits, families receive guidance on child development, parenting support, and strategies to strengthen the bond between parents and their children. Parents are acknowledged as their child's first and most important teachers, and this program is designed to enhance that role.
 Parents as Teachers aims to walk alongside families, offering support rather than directing them.
 If you are interested in the Parents as Teachers program, please call (423) 209-8298 or visit health.hamiltontn.org/…/childse…/parentsasteachers(pat).aspx.

items.content_text:
Even as they get older, younger generations across #OECD countries continue to have lower homeownership rates than older generations.  
  This is due to rising house prices, particularly in large cities, which are making it increasingly difficult for younger and lower-wealth households to enter the housing market.  
 As owning a home has traditionally been a key pathway to building wealth, the decline in homeownership trend also risks widening wealth gaps over generations.  
 OECD analysis explores recent trends in household wealth, highlights significant wealth gaps across different population groups. It also shows how better individual-level data collection could improve measurement and better inform efforts to address wealth inequality.  
 Following #InternationalYouthDay, explore one of the major economic challenges facing younger generations: https://brnw.ch/21x4TEl | #OECDyouth

items.content_text:
Anthropology major Tom Laufenberg and 2025 graduate Faith Johnson joined visiting lecturer AJ Van Slyke and an international team of researchers in Jamaica to survey the waters surrounding the submerged city of Port Royal. 
 Using remote-sensing and underwater archaeology techniques, the team investigated areas identified through centuries-old historical records. Their work led to the identification of HMS Aboukir, a British warship that had been missing since 1881. The expedition was featured on Discovery Channel’s “Expedition Unknown,” highlighting the research and collaboration behind the search.
 The experience also continues to shape research in Chattanooga, where the team is now applying its skills to the submerged town of Old Harrison beneath Chickamauga Lake.
 🔗  Read the full story: https://blog.utc.edu/…/discovery-channels-expedition-unkno…/

The Urban League of Greater Chattanooga is deeply saddened to share the news of the passing of our beloved supporter and longtime consultant, BettyLynn Smith. BettyLynn's journey with us began under the guidance of former President/CEO Warren Logan, where she quickly became known as his invaluable right hand in advancing our mission of empowering communities and transforming lives.
 Her dedication and passion were instrumental in the development and success of our flagship initiative, the Inclusion by Design Program. This program equips senior leaders with the tools necessary to develop inclusive environments and enhance organizational performance, a true testament to BettyLynn's commitment to creating positive change.
 Beyond her work with the Urban League, BettyLynn was a pioneer; her influence was felt as a founder of the Black Professionals at the Hunter Museum. She also took pride in her membership with Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, Incorporated, embodying the values of service and sisterhood in everything she did.
 BettyLynn's spirit and contributions have left an indelible mark on our organization and the community we serve. She will be profoundly missed by all of us at the Urban League, and our hearts go out to her family during this difficult time. BettyLynn's legacy will continue to inspire us as we carry forward the work she so passionately championed.

items.title: Exploring Downtown: The Tivoli Theatre When the Tivoli opened its doors in 1921, it was quickly given the name "Jewel of...
items.content_text:
Exploring Downtown: The Tivoli Theatre
 When the Tivoli opened its doors in 1921, it was quickly given the name "Jewel of the South". Created by renowned architects Rapp & Rapp alongside Chattanooga architect R.H. Hunt, it featured ornate interiors, crystal chandeliers, a grand lobby, and the Mighty Wurlitzer pipe organ that still calls the Tivoli home today. It was also one of the first air-conditioned public buildings in the South, making it a destination for audiences from across the region.
 As modern cinemas rose in popularity during the 1950s, the Tivoli faced decline. But Chattanooga rallied behind its landmark. It reopened as a community cultural center in 1963, was purchased by the City of Chattanooga in 1976 to preserve its future, and underwent a major restoration before reopening in 1989 as the city's premier performing arts venue. In 2015, the Tivoli Theatre Foundation was formed to operate and preserve the historic theater, in addition to two other sites: the Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Auditorium, and the Walker Theatre. 
 Today, the Tivoli is once again in the midst of a historic transformation. The restoration that began in 2022 isn't just about renovating a building, it's about preserving the craftsmanship, history, and memories that have defined this iconic theater for generations. When the Tivoli welcomes audiences back, it will continue the legacy that has made it the heart of Chattanooga's performing arts scene for more than a century.

Historic preservation is about more than protecting buildings. It’s about preserving the places that tell the story of our communities.

We’re excited to congratulate Polk County on receiving $60,000 in Federal Historic Preservation Fund grant funding from the Tennessee Historical Commission to support restoration of the historic Polk County Courthouse in Benton.

This investment builds on an additional $500,000 Historic Development Grant Program award for the courthouse, which will support restroom renovations on all floors and restoration of the building’s distinctive Art Deco doors and windows.

We’re also proud to recognize SETD Historic Preservation Planner Stefanie Haire, Ph.D. for her work alongside Polk County to help secure this funding and advance the preservation of an important historic asset in our region.

Congratulations to Polk County, Stefanie, and all of the partners helping preserve this landmark for generations to come.

📄 Read the full Tennessee Historical Commission announcement: https://lnkd.in/guf7x-Rx

COLLEGEDALE, TN – City officials, administrative staff, and employees of the City of Collegedale invite the community to gather on September 10, 2026 at 6:30 p.m. in the Municipal Courtroom of Collegedale City Hall, located at 4910 Swinyar Dr., to honor the life of service lived by Judge Kevin B. Wilson.  
 A dedicated public servant, Judge Wilson was first elected as City of Collegedale Court Judge in 1990 and served faithfully until his passing on January 9, 2026. Known for his fairness and steady presence on the bench, he left a lasting mark on the Collegedale community.  
 "Judge Wilson gave so much of himself to this community and this court," said Collegedale Municipal Court Clerk Rachel Shuttles. "This dedication is a chance for all of us who knew him, and everyone he served, to come together in his honor." 
 The ceremony will give the community an opportunity to reflect on Judge Wilson’s legacy and celebrate his years of service to the City of Collegedale. A reception with light refreshments will follow.

items.title: After years of service protecting the Chattanooga community, the Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is honoring the ret...
items.content_text:
After years of service protecting the Chattanooga community, the Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is honoring the retirement of two members of its K9 Unit: K9 Burt, a decorated patrol and narcotics detection dog, and K9 Duke, who ultimately found his true calling outside of police work.
 K9 Burt, an 11-year-old Belgian Malinois, retired after 10 years of distinguished service with the CPD. As a narcotics detection canine, Burt was responsible for locating more than $3 million in illegal narcotics and currency during his career. Among his most significant contributions were three separate cases in which he located more than 1,000 fentanyl pills.
 “K9 Burt exemplified the courage and reliability that every handler hopes for in a partner,” said MPO Luke Timmons, Burt’s handler. “What makes me most proud is that no officers were ever injured by suspects during any of Burt’s deployments.”
 Having a single handler for an entire working career is a rarity among police K9s, making the partnership between Burt and Timmons even stronger. 
 Burt also earned recognition beyond Chattanooga for his exceptional performance in training and competition. He was named the United States Police Canine Association (USPCA) Regional Top Dog in both narcotics detection and dual-purpose certifications. During the USPCA Detector Dog Challenge, Burt earned first place honors in the room-search portion of the competition before an untimely bathroom break during the vehicle-search event derailed his chances at the overall title - even elite, highly trained police dogs go when they have to go.
 While K9 Duke’s career followed a different, less illustrious path, he will be remembered as part of the Chattanooga Police Department family.
 Despite many months of extensive training sessions, Duke consistently demonstrated that police work was not of interest to him. Ultimately, the K9 Unit retired Duke early and found him a loving home. Duke was originally purchased using grant funding, and all grant requirements were satisfied before his early retirement.
 The Chattanooga Police Department thanks both K9 Burt and K9 Duke for their time with the department and recognizes the commitment of the handlers, families, and community members who support the K9 Unit.
 The Chattanooga Police Department wishes both K9s a long, healthy retirement.
